25 A police car has a two-tone siren emitting sound of frequencies of 700 Hz and 1000 Hz.
The police car is travelling at a speed of 40.0 m s–1 towards a stationary observer. The speed of
sound in the air is 340 m s–1.
What is the difference between the two frequencies of the sound that is heard by the observer?
A
268 Hz
B
300 Hz
C
335 Hz
D
340 Hz

hints: Notice the source speed $40.0 \text{ m s}^{-1}$ towards the stationary observer shortens the observed wavelength for both the $700 \text{ Hz}$ and $1000 \text{ Hz}$ tones.
Recall the approaching-source Doppler factor $v/(v - v_s)$ with $v = 340 \text{ m s}^{-1}$, so both heard frequencies are higher by the same factor.
Calculate the heard difference as $(1000-700)$ multiplied by that factor, rather than subtracting $300 \text{ Hz}$ at the end without scaling.
walkthrough: Identify the given data: emitted frequencies $f_1 = 700 \text{ Hz}$ and $f_2 = 1000 \text{ Hz}$, source speed $v_s = 40.0 \text{ m s}^{-1}$ towards observer, wave speed $v = 340 \text{ m s}^{-1}$.
State the Doppler rule for source approaching stationary observer: $f_o = f_s \times v/(v - v_s)$ because wavefronts are crowded together.
Apply to the frequency difference directly: $\Delta f_o = (1000 - 700) \times 340/300$.
Substitute and calculate: $\Delta f_o = 300 \times 340/300 = 340 \text{ Hz}$ with unit $\text{Hz}$, larger than the emitted $300 \text{ Hz}$ as expected for approach.

A.explanation: This is $300 \times 340/380$, the difference if the car were moving away at $40.0 \text{ m s}^{-1}$, not towards the observer.

B.explanation: This is $1000 - 700$, the emitted difference with no Doppler shift applied to either $700 \text{ Hz}$ or $1000 \text{ Hz}$ tone.

C.explanation: This is close to the correct value but does not equal $(1000-700) \times 340/(340-40)$ evaluated correctly.

D.explanation: Both observed frequencies are scaled by $340/(340-40)$, so the observed difference is $300 \times 340/300 = 340 \text{ Hz}$.
